title: Focal length vs camera position — Image Wiki
text:
Focal length vs camera position
  Where the camera stands decides how big near things look next to far things. The lens only decides how much of that view fits in the frame.

  
    Termperspective vs focal length
    Also calledlens compression, perspective distortion, wide-angle distortion, foreshortening
    Not the same asbarrel distortion, field of view, depth of field
    Read7 min
  

  
    
      On this page
      
        Why it happensThe test that ends the argumentSo where does compression come fromWhat focal length genuinely changesBarrel distortion is a different defectCommon mistakes
      
    
  

  Take a selfie at arm's length and your nose comes out too big. Hand the phone to someone across the room, have them zoom until your head fills the same amount of frame, and you look like yourself again.
Almost everybody blames the lens, and that is wrong. Perspective — the relative size of near things and far things — is set by where the camera is and only by that. The lens decides how much of the view lands inside the frame.
Why it happens
Apparent size falls off with distance, so what shapes an object is not the distance to it but the ratio of the distances to its near part and its far part.
At selfie distance the tip of your nose is maybe 30 cm from the lens and your ears about 40 cm. Ratio 1.33, so the nose gets drawn a third bigger relative to the ears than it should be. Step back to two metres: 200 cm and 210 cm, ratio 1.05, and the face flattens out. No glass changed. The ratio changed.

Two posts of the same real height, 2 m apart. The only thing that changes between panels is where the camera stands.
Top: at 1 m the far post is 3 m away — three times as far as the near one — so it is drawn a third the size. Bottom: from 4 m the distances are 4 m and 6 m, a ratio of 1.5, and the posts come out nearly the same size. The lens change is a consequence: keeping the near post the same size from four times further back takes roughly four times the focal length.




Close, wide lens: 17 mm
Far, long lens: 200 mm


Armin Kübelbeck, 2008, from a series at seven focal lengths with the subject held the same size in the frame. Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 3.0.
Her head is about the same width in both. Now compare the feet, the nearest thing to the camera. At 17 mm one foot is wider than her head and the legs run away down a long stretch of jeans; at 200 mm a foot is about as wide as her head, and the legs have collapsed to almost nothing.


The test that ends the argument
Photography Life shot a bridge from a tripod at 24 mm and at 70 mm, then cropped the 24 mm frame to the 70 mm framing — a 285% enlargement, so it looks terrible, and the geometry is identical: same bridge shape, pier railing in the same place. Photograph people at 11 mm on full frame from a sane distance and crop in hard and they look normal too: the super-wide lens distorted nobody, because the camera was not close to anybody.
If your feet do not move, changing focal length does exactly what cropping does, minus the lost pixels.
So where does compression come from
From standing far away. Photography Life shot one person at 24, 70, 105, 200 and 300 mm, backing up each time to hold her size in the frame; her distance to the background never changed, and by 300 mm two planters 10 m apart looked almost stacked.


24 mm, close to the subject
400 mm, far from the subject


Florian Schott, 2007, same footbridge, same f/5.6, subject held the same size in the frame. Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 3.0.
Follow the handrail she is leaning on. At 24 mm it runs away down the bridge deck to a vanishing point and brings the whole gorge with it: conifers on the far side drawn small, the rock face beyond them smaller still. At 400 mm that handrail crosses the lower frame almost flat, and the rock face — which never moved — fills the whole background and reads as a wall close behind her.
She is the same size in both, so it is the background magnification that changed. The softer rendering on the right is a second consequence of shooting from far back with a long lens; see Depth of field.


The lens gets the credit for this because of a habit: you reach for a long lens when you cannot get close, and a wide one when you cannot get back.
What focal length genuinely changes

Angle of view — how wide a wedge of the world lands in the frame. Everything else follows from this, magnification from a fixed spot included.
How much background sits behind your subject, and how large each object in it is drawn.
The distance you end up standing at for a given framing — the indirect route to every perspective effect above, and the reason 70-135 mm is called the portrait range.
Handheld sharpness. Long lenses magnify your own shake; the rule of thumb is a shutter of at least 1/focal length seconds on 35 mm.
Depth of field from a fixed position at the same f-number — see Depth of field, and Exposure and dynamic range for what an f-number costs elsewhere.

Barrel distortion is a different defect
Optical distortion is real, measurable and unrelated to all of the above: the lens fails to draw straight lines straight, barrel bowing them outward from the centre, pincushion pulling them inward. Wide zooms are the usual offenders. Look for it on brickwork, window frames, tiled floors, a sea horizon near the top of the frame. It is also small — the Nikon 50mm f/1.4G has roughly 1.4% barrel distortion, obvious on bricks and doing essentially nothing to a face. Photography Life's conclusion is that even the worst-distorting lens will not distort a subject kept away from the camera.
One more wide-angle effect is neither of these. A rectilinear lens keeps straight lines straight by stretching the corners, so a face near the edge of a very wide shot comes out egg-shaped and broad-shouldered. That is the flat projection, not a fault in the glass, and it survives the crop test.
Common mistakes

"A wide lens distorts faces." Standing 30 cm from a face distorts it. Filling the frame with a face is what puts you at 30 cm.
"85mm is a flattering focal length." The focal length is a proxy for the working distance it forces on you. An 85 mm portrait flatters because you shot it from two metres.
"A telephoto compresses the background." Distance compresses it. The telephoto is what lets you be that far away and still frame the subject.
"Zooming in is the same as walking closer." Zooming changes framing. Walking changes shape. Zoom from where you stand and every relative size stays exactly as it was.
"Converging verticals mean a wide lens." They mean the camera was tilted up or down. Aim at the horizon and verticals stay parallel with any lens — which is what an architectural shift lens exploits, sliding the frame upward inside an oversized image circle instead of tilting the camera.


How to read camera position out of a photo

Find something whose real proportions you know: a face, a car, a doorway. Near parts oversized against far parts means a close camera, and nothing else.
Look at the scale of the background. Distant buildings or hills rendered huge behind the subject means the camera was far back with a long lens.
Check the straight lines. Bowed near the edges is barrel or pincushion, a lens defect. Converging is camera tilt.
Do steps 1 and 2 agree? Close-up proportions on a subject in front of a compressed, telephoto-looking background is a strong sign of two images stitched together. Check the shadow edges on both halves too (Hard and soft light).
